catalog_quote: STRESS The stress system of Ojibwe has been analyzed by a number of researchers (Bloomfield 1958, Rhodes 1976, Valentine 1985, etc.). Basically, the system is one of quantity sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge of the word, i.e., a preferred rhythm of weak-strong, in which the weak position m a y only be filled by a short vowel. The final syllable is often analyzed as extrametrical. Very similar stress systems have been proposed for other Algonquian languages, e.g., Passamaquoddy (Stowell 1979). In southeastern dialects of Ojibwe, a very prominent mle of weak vowel syncope is resulting in a restructuring of m u c h of the lexicon and the form of inflectional person prefixes on verbs and nouns. In other dialects, such as Berens River Ojibwe, the same quantity-sensitive iambic metrical patterns are evident, but the correlate of stress in these dialects is pitch, resulting in al…

sources.quote: 'According to Rhodes (1985), stress in Proto-Algonquian falls on even-numbered syllables counting from left to right; syllables with long vowels, however, are always stressed, with the alternating pattern restarting to their right.
